extra.message: NoSQL injection leading to authentication bypass in POST /api/users. When req.body.password contains '{', it is passed through JSON.parse() (line 31) and used directly as the password value in the MongoDB query object 'searchstring', which is executed by dbase.collection('login').find(searchstring) (line 44). An attacker can submit 'email=admin@xvna.com&password={"$ne": "wrong"}' so the executed query becomes find({email: 'admin@xvna.com', password: {$ne: 'wrong'}}), which matches the stored admin document and returns 'true' (line 50) without knowing the real password. req.body.email is likewise interpolated into the query unsanitized.

NoSQL injection in GET /getdata. The 'id' query parameter is parsed with JSON.parse (line 83) and used directly as the query value in dbase.collection('users').find({ id: id }, ...) (line 87). An attacker can request /getdata?id={"$ne": null} (or $gt, $regex, $where operators) to make the query match arbitrary documents and dump every user record; the injected value is also reflected back in the response as 'search: id' (line 90).

NoSQL injection in POST /insecure_dor. req.body.accountno (line 138) is used unsanitized as the query value in dbase.collection('a5_insecure_dor').find({ accountno: accno }) (line 142). Because bodyParser.json()/urlencoded(extended) preserve object types, an attacker can POST {"accountno": {"$ne": ""}} to match and return every account record in the collection instead of a single one.

NoSQL injection in POST /a6_misconfig. JSON.parse(req.body.accountno) (line 179) lets an attacker supply an arbitrary JSON object that is used directly in dbase.collection('a5_insecure_dor').find({ accountno: accno }) (line 186). Sending {"accountno": {"$ne": ""}} matches all documents and discloses every account; operators such as $gt, $regex and $where can also be injected into the MongoDB query.

OS command injection in GET /ping. The 'id' query parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command: exec('ping ' + id, ...) (line 155). child_process.exec runs its argument through /bin/sh, so a request like /ping?id=127.0.0.1;cat%20/etc/passwd (or '&&', backticks, '$(...)') executes arbitrary operating-system commands on the server, and stdout/stderr are returned to the attacker in the response (lines 156-158).

Remote code execution via eval injection in GET /eval. The 'id' and 'id2' query parameters (lines 200-201) are concatenated and passed to eval(id + id2) (line 202). An attacker can request /eval?id=process&id2=.binding('process').mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id').toString() to execute arbitrary JavaScript (and via child_process, arbitrary OS commands) on the server with the Node.js process privileges, and the result is returned in the JSON response.

Reflected cross-site scripting in GET /xss_r. The raw 'id' query parameter (line 163) is used in a MongoDB lookup and echoed back verbatim to the client in the JSON response as 'search: id' (line 170) without any sanitization or HTML encoding. The frontend (public/app/js/controllers/a7_xss_reflected.js line 7) feeds this reflected value to $sce.trustAsHtml() and renders it with ng-bind-html, so a crafted link such as /xss_r?id= executes attacker-controlled script in the victim's browser.

The endpoint looks up records in the 'a5_insecure_dor' collection using the client-supplied 'accountno' (lines 138, 142) and returns the full account document (name, account number, account type) via res.json(result) (line 145) without any authentication, session check, or ownership verification. extra.message: Missing authentication for all sensitive API endpoints. The only authentication logic, POST /service_login (lines 60-70), is registered as a standalone route instead of middleware, so it guards nothing. None of the data-handling routes (/getdata, /a3sensitive, /a3sensitive_header, /ping, /xss_r, /insecure_dor, /a6_misconfig, /eval, /insecure_deserialization) performs any session or authorization check; the client-side redirect to the login page ($state.go('access.login') in dashboard.js) is purely cosmetic and trivially bypassed by calling the APIs directly.

extra.message: Exposure of sensitive information in GET /a3sensitive. The query dbase.collection('users').find({ id: parseInt(id) }) (line 103) has no field projection, so the complete user document - including the stored 'password' field (see collection/users.json) - is serialized to the caller in res.json({cmd: result, search: id}) (line 106). Combined with the total absence of authentication on this route, any caller can enumerate id=1,2,3,... and retrieve other users' login credentials in plaintext.

extra.message: Information disclosure through header reflection in GET /a3sensitive_header. The endpoint returns the complete set of HTTP request headers to the client via res.send(JSON.stringify(req.headers)) (line 116) without authentication. This echoes back sensitive headers such as Cookie (session identifiers), Authorization credentials, and any internal reverse-proxy/infrastructure headers, providing an information-exposure oracle that amplifies other attacks (e.g., session cookie theft when combined with the XSS findings).

Information exposure through error messages in POST /a6_misconfig. Both the MongoDB connection error (res.json(err), line 183) and the collection query error (res.json(err), line 188) are returned verbatim to the client. Raw driver error objects disclose internal details such as the database host/port, connection state, and query structure. Additionally, after a failed connection the code continues using the null 'db' object, causing an unhandled exception and crash of the request handler.

extra.message: Plaintext credentials stored in a web-served file. public/users.xml contains user logins and passwords in cleartext (e.g., <login>raj</login><password>kumar</password>, lines 5-6). index.js mounts the entire directory with app.use(express.static('public')) (index.js line 5), so the file is downloadable at http://<host>/users.xml by any unauthenticated visitor, directly disclosing application credentials.

Insecure deserialization of user-influenced data in POST /insecure_deserialization. The request-controlled value req.body.userid (line 208) is embedded into an object that is round-tripped through the node-serialize 0.0.4 package: serialize.serialize(obj) (line 216) followed by serialize.unserialize(objS) (line 218). node-serialize's unserialize() reconstructs '_$$ND_FUNC$$_'-prefixed values using eval/new Function, and the package carries a known remote-code-execution advisory (CVE-2017-5941); passing data derived from user input through it allows an attacker who can influence the serialized payload to achieve arbitrary code execution.

Hardcoded session signing secret. express-session is initialized with secret: "Your secret key" (line 14). The secret is committed to the repository, so anyone with access to the source can forge validly-signed session cookies and impersonate any logged-in user (the login handler stores req.session.user, index.js line 49, and all authorization relies solely on this session). The session cookie is additionally configured without secure, httpOnly hardening, or a store, compounding the weakness.
